system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-06-20 07:35:00 to 2187-06-26 13:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a complex history including Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, SVC repair, and HIT was readmitted with bloody diarrhea, fever, and vomiting. She had recently completed a course of levofloxacin for pneumonia. Evaluation supported a Crohn’s flare, with elevated inflammatory markers and negative stool studies for infection. She was managed with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. Due to extensive venous occlusive disease, IV access was lost and could not be reestablished, prompting a transition to oral and rectal medications. Given her severe anxiety and PTSD, she elected for early discharge after tolerating oral hydromorphone and rectal promethazine. She was discharged home on antibiotics, analgesics, and continued fondaparinux, with close follow-up advised.

INDICATION:  Abdominal pain, evaluate for obstruction.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiographs from ___ and ___.

FINDINGS:  There is marked gaseous distention of the colon measuring up to
10.9 cm in caliber.  While there are no definite dilated loops of small bowel,
this cannot be excluded.  No evidence of free air.  An NG tube is seen ending
in the gastric cardia.  The NG tube side port ends within the distal
esophagus.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Marked gaseous distention of the colon with possible dilatation of the
small bowel.  While these findings could represent chronic ileus, the
possibility of obstruction cannot be excluded.

2.  No evidence of pneumoperitoneum.

3.  The NG tube side port ends in the distal esophagus and should be advanced.

Pertinent findings were discussed with Dr. ___ by Dr. ___ at 8:15
a.m. on the day of the study.

INDICATION:  Abdominal distention with dilated loops on KUB, assess for
obstruction.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT-acquired axial images were obtained from the lung bases to
pubic symphysis after oral but not IV contrast.  Coronal and sagittal
reformations were prepared.

COMPARISONS:  KUB from earlier the same day and CT abdomen and pelvis from
___.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITH CONTRAST:  The imaged lung bases demonstrate right
middle lobar scarring without pleural or pericardial effusion.

The evaluation of the solid and visceral organs in the abdomen is limited in
the absence of intravenous contrast. Nasogastric tube courses into the
stomach.  The liver is normal in attenuation without focal lesion, intra- or
extra-hepatic biliary ductal dilatation.  The gallbladder is surgically
absent.  The pancreas, spleen, bilateral adrenal glands, and kidneys are
unremarkable without hydronephrosis.  The stomach and small bowel are grossly
unremarkable, without dilated or decompressed loops to suggest obstruction.
The large bowel is diffusely distended containing air and stool without mural
thickening or adjacent stranding to suggest colitis.  Changes from prior
partial colectomy are noted in the right mid abdomen.  There is no free air or
free fluid in the abdomen.  There is no pathologic mesenteric or
retroperitoneal adenopathy though numerous prominent right mesenteric nodes
are again noted.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH CONTRAST:  The bladder and rectum are unremarkable.  The
uterus is surgically absent.  No pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy or free
fluid.

OSSEOUS AND SOFT TISSUE STRUCTURES:  There is no lytic or sclerotic bony
lesion concerning for osseous malignant process.  Bilateral gluteal injection
granulomata are noted.  Gas in the soft tissues of the anterior right
abdominal wall is likely from injection.

IMPRESSION:  Distended loops of large bowel containing air and stool suggest
colonic ileus without evidence of small bowel obstruction.  

This was discussed with by Dr. ___ by Dr. ___ at 13:25 on ___.

INDICATION:  Evaluate for lower gastrointestinal obstruction.

COMPARISONS:  CT abdomen, ___.

GASTROGRAFIN ENEMA:  Under fluoroscopic guidance, Gastrografin was instilled
into the rectum and sigmoid colon.  Rectum and sigmoid colon appeared normal
in course and contour with some filling defects due to stool.  There were no
strictures or diverticula or evidence of leaks.  Contrast appeared to reach
the distal descending colon and then stop.  There was no evidence of tapering
to suggest stricture or tethering.  This was likely due to stool impaction as
seen on the CT scan.  The patient was starting to feel somewhat uncomfortable,
so the Gastrografin was removed and the study stopped.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of rectal or sigmoid strictures or obstruction. 
Gastrografin unable to pass the distal descending colon, likely due to stool
impaction.

INDICATION:  Replaced NG tube.

COMPARISON:  ___.

PORTABLE CHEST:

Sternotomy wires are in unchanged alignment.  There is a new nasogastric tube,
which reaches the stomach, though the sideholes remain in the distal
esophagus, and this should be advanced for optimal positioning.

There is increased vascular congestion and perihilar opacity, suggesting mild
pulmonary edema.  There is stable linear scarring in the right mid lung. There
is no effusion.  There is no pneumothorax.  There is no convincing evidence of

IMPRESSION:  

Nasogastric tube reaches the stomach, but needs to be advanced for optimal
position.

Increased  mild pulmonary edema.

Dr. ___ was paged with these findings on ___ at 10:30
a.m. by Dr. ___ phone.

INDICATION:  History of Crohn's with fever.  Concerning for pneumonia.  Query
consolidation.

TECHNIQUE:  Single upright portable view of the chest.

COMPARISON:  Compared with prior radiographs through ___ to ___.

FINDINGS:  The tip of the orogastric tube is at T4 vertebral level.  Consider
repositioning the orogastric tube.  Since ___, right upper and mid lung
opacities have worsened whereas right lower lobe opacity is new.  The left
lung is clear.  The heart size, mediastinal and hilar contours are normal. 
The patient is status post median sternotomy and sternal sutures are intact.

IMPRESSION:  Since ___, right upper lobe opacities are worse whereas
right lower lobe opacity is new.  Possibilities include interval worsening of
lung infection or aspiration. Follow up radiograph is recommended after a day
to look for interval changes and to differentiate between both.

The radiographic record shows persisting right upper lobe consolidation due to
indolent infection since ___ in the region of pre-existing mild
bronchiectasis, documented by CT as early as ___.  A second, smaller region
of peribronchial opacification in the right lower lobe, new or increased since
___, has a distribution more common for aspiration and may or may not be
related to upper lobe infection.  The previous report should not have read
'tuberculosis is most likely', but should have read 'depending on clinical
circumstances, tuberculosis should be considered.'  If there is no particular
clinical concern for tuberculosis, the radiographic findings though not
diagnostic of tuberculosis, raise the possibility of that pathogen (and
non-tuberculous mycobacteria) among other persistent infections.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH

TECHNIQUE:  Portable AP upright radiograph was compared with prior chest
radiographs through ___ with the most recent from ___.

FINDINGS:

OGT terminates few centimeters below the gastroesophageal junction.  Consider
advancing it further for better seating.  Since ___, right upper and mid
lung opacities have increased, whereas right lower lobe opacity is new. Left
lung is clear. Heart size, mediastinal and hilar contours are normal.  Patient
is status post median sternotomy and sternal sutures are intact.  There is no
pleural effusion.

IMPRESSION:

Since ___, right upper and mid lung opacities have increased and right
lower lobe opacity is new, suggesting worsening infection.  Given the clinical
setting, tuberculosis is most likely.

PROCEDURE: RIGHT GREAT SAPHENOUS VEIN PICC PLACEMENT: ___.

INDICATION:  ___ year-old woman with fever and no venous access. She requires
venous access for hydration and possible antibiotics and TPN.

RADIOLOGISTS:  Dr. ___ (fellow) and Dr. ___
(attending physician) performed the procedure.

ANESTHESIA:  General anesthesia was provided by the anesthesia team.

TECHNIQUE/FINDINGS:

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient after explaining the
procedure, benefits, risks, and alternatives.  The patient was brought to the
angiography suite, positioned supine on the table, and placed under
anesthesia. The right groin and upper thigh area were prepped and draped in a
sterile fashion.  A preprocedural huddle and timeout were performed per ___
protocol.

The right great saphenous vein was accessed under ultrasound guidance with a
micropuncture needle.  An ultrasound image of the patent vein was saved to the
archive. A 0.018 inch guidewire was advanced through the needle, which was
able to be advance up to the saphenofemoral junction.  Then, the needle was
exchanged for a micropuncture sheath.  Once the sheath was in place, the inner
dilator and guidewire were removed and a 0.035 inch Glidewire was utilized to
reach the IVC-RA junction.  Then, the micropuncture sheath was exchanged for a
4 ___ MPA catheter, which was threaded over the wire to the IVC-RA
junction.  Then, the Glidewire was exchanged for the 0.018 inch guidewire. 
The MPA catheter was exchanged for a 5.5 ___ peel-away sheath.  With the
peel-away sheath in place, a 57 cm PICC was advanced over the wire.  The PICC
did not pass central to the saphenofemoral junction, so a SV8 wire was
introduced into the second lumen of the ___ double-lumen PICC and this
was again advanced to the IVC-RA junction.  Then, the existing 0.018 guidewire
was removed, and the PICC was advanced over the SV8 wire with its tip at the
IVC-right atrium junction.  A stored fluoroscopic image was saved to the
archive. Both lumens withdrew and flushed well.  The PICC was secured to the
skin using a StatLock and Tegaderms.  The patient tolerated the procedure
well.  There were no immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:

Placement of a 5 ___, 57 cm double-lumen PICC through the right great
saphenous vein with its tip lying at the IVC-RA junction.  The PICC is ready
to use.

STUDY:  PA and lateral chest, ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  A ___ woman with possible pneumonia.  Evaluate for
interval change.

FINDINGS:  Comparison is made to previous study from ___.

The cardiac silhouette and mediastinum is normal.  Mediastinal wires are seen.
There is again seen hazy areas of consolidation in the right upper lobe and
the right base, which is unchanged from prior.  The left lung appears well
aerated.  There has been removal of the nasogastric tube since the prior
study.  No pleural effusions are seen, and there are no pneumothoraces.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because of abdominal pain and distention. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I woke up last night with sharp pain and a lot of bloating. It felt like my old bowel obstructions. I’ve had Crohn’s for years and multiple surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were here two days ago with similar symptoms. The CT scan shows your colon is very distended with air and stool, but no blockage. This looks like an ileus—your bowel isn’t moving properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not another obstruction? That’s a relief. But why is this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history of Crohn’s and many abdominal surgeries, your bowel motility can be unpredictable. We’ll manage this conservatively—no food for now, IV fluids, and we’ll keep the NG tube to help decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I placed the NG tube myself in the ER. It helps, but it’s uncomfortable. Will I need it long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it until your bowels start moving again. Once you pass gas or have a bowel movement, we can consider removing it and slowly restart your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been feeling a bit short of breath. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray, and there’s some consolidation in your right lung. It could be pneumonia or from aspiration. We’ll start antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspiration? I did vomit a little last night. But I’m not running a fever now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain it. Even without fever, we treat it because of your medical history. We’ll use levofloxacin instead of cipro, since you’re allergic to many antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have a long list. I’m also on fondaparinux for my HIT history. Will you continue that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll keep your home dose for blood clot prevention, especially since you’re not moving much right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your white blood cell count is low, and you’re mildly anemic. We’re watching that. Any gas or bowel movement yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I passed some gas last night, but no bowel movement. The bloating is still there, but maybe a little less?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Passing gas means your bowel is starting to wake up. We’ll keep the NG tube for now but may try a Gastrografin enema tomorrow to help move things along.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An enema? I’ve had those before. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be uncomfortable, but we’ll go slow. It helps us see if there’s a blockage and can also stimulate the bowel. The CT didn’t show a stricture, so we’re hopeful it’s just stool slowing things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Gastrografin enema was stopped early—you were getting uncomfortable, and the contrast only reached the descending colon. It looks like stool impaction is holding things up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stricture from Crohn’s? That’s good. Can we do something to clear the stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO for now and let the Gastrografin work. It can act as a laxative. We’ll also keep the NG tube to suction to keep your stomach decompressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really tired. My labs showed low white count—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count has been dropping, but your blood cultures are negative. No infection is growing. It may be related to your Crohn’s or medications. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your chest X-ray shows the pneumonia is stable. But we’re still concerned because the right upper lobe opacity hasn’t improved. We’re continuing levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I read one report said tuberculosis is possible. Is that true?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiologist mentioned it as a possibility because of the chronic appearance, but there’s no evidence you have symptoms of TB. Your PCP will follow up after discharge to decide if more testing is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’m also worried about IV access. I’ve had line infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line in your right leg vein under ultrasound guidance. It’s secure and ready to use. This avoids using your arm veins, which are compromised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel safer knowing it’s in a new spot. How’s my belly doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a small bowel movement this morning! That’s a big step. We’ll try removing the NG tube later if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Can I try sipping water then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once the NG is out and you’re not nauseated, we’ll start clear liquids and advance slowly. Your gastroenterologist recommends continuing cipro and flagyl for your Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight—no nausea, passed gas again, and your abdomen is less distended. We’re removing the NG tube now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I can finally breathe easier without it. Can I eat real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids and soft foods. Given your short bowel syndrome, we’ll go slow to avoid overwhelming your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My anxiety’s been worse being in the hospital. Can I have my oxazepam? I lost my pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll prescribe a replacement. We know your PTSD makes hospital stays harder. We’ll keep your anxiety meds available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two soft bowel movements and tolerated a full diet. Your lungs are clear, and vitals are stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue fondaparinux, levothyroxine, and sertraline. For pain, hydromorphone as needed. Promethazine for nausea, oxazepam for anxiety, and Nascobal nasal spray weekly for B12.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The levofloxacin is complete—five days. Your pneumonia is resolving. Your gastroenterologist will decide if you need cipro and flagyl longer as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your PCP and gastroenterologist soon. They’ll review the lung findings and your Crohn’s management. Call us if you have fever, severe pain, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad this wasn’t another surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Your ileus resolved with conservative care, and your pneumonia improved with antibiotics. You’ve done really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable, and you walked to the lounge without issues. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better. I’ll take it easy and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember to take your meds, stay hydrated, and reach out if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care and get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I definitely will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge nurse will go over your prescriptions and instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. You’ve come a long way in just over a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels like it. I’m just grateful it wasn’t worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your resilience helps. Keep listening to your body and following up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye for now.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a complex history including Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, multiple prior surgeries, and PTSD was admitted for abdominal pain and distention. Imaging revealed colonic ileus without obstruction, and she was managed conservatively with NG tube decompression, NPO status, and pain control. She also had community-acquired pneumonia with right upper lobe consolidation, treated with a 5-day course of levofloxacin. Her bowel function gradually improved, allowing NG tube removal and diet advancement. A PICC line was placed for reliable access due to her history of line infections and venous compromise. She stabilized, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home with prescriptions for pain, nausea, anxiety, and anticoagulation, with plans for outpatient follow-up on her lung findings and Crohn’s management.
